title: Reverse a backwards-running three-phase conveyor motor by swapping two supply leads
instruction: This conveyor's motor was just replaced and now runs backwards. Rearrange the supply leads among the terminal box's three sockets so that the conveyor runs the way the arrows on its guard point, with every plug pushed fully home, then let go. The supply is isolated; it is switched on once you are clear.
context: Electricians (O*NET 47-2111) correct a motor that runs the wrong way by exchanging any two of its three supply leads; with single-pole camlock connectors on temporary power, that means swapping two plugs. Moving all three one place along keeps the phase sequence and changes nothing, and here the leads start in colour order, so tidying them changes nothing either.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left); everything except the leads and the tote is fixed (screwed or taped down). Terminal box: blue-grey PLA box 6 (x) x 18 (y) x 4.5 cm tall, front face at x 36, centred on y 0, standing on the table. In its front face, at table level, three single-pole power sockets (like camlock connectors) 22 mm wide x 19 mm tall x 26 mm deep, centred at y +5 (U), 0 (V) and -5 (W) (in the real build each socket also has a sprung side contact that grips the plug's tip pin; README, Real-world build). Motor: blue-grey PLA cylinder (the motor's housing) 8 cm across and 14 cm long, axis along y, centred at x 46, y 0, resting on the table behind the box. Gearbox: dark grey PLA block 6 x 6 x 8 cm tall at x 43 to 49, y -9 to -15, coupled to the motor; on its front face a white PLA pointer disc 5 cm across, 4 mm thick, with a red stripe from its centre to the top; a steel shaft from its back into the conveyor. Conveyor: light grey aluminium bed 10 (x) x 40 (y) x 5 cm tall centred at x 63, y 0, with a black rubber belt on top; along its front a yellow PLA guard plate 5 x 40 cm, 5.2 cm tall (x 53 to 58), carrying two black painted arrows pointing to the robot's right (-y), a red tape line across it at y +6 and a green tape line at y -6. Tote: blue PLA box 6 (x) x 8 (y) x 4 cm, 150 g, on the belt centred at y 0. Gland plate: dark grey PLA block 3 x 16 x 3 cm tall at x 12 to 15, centred on y 0. Leads: three 6 mm round PVC leads 24 cm long, brown (L1), black (L2) and grey (L3), leaving the gland plate's back face at y +5, 0 and -5, each ending in a plug body 55 x 16 x 14 mm (ABS, the lead's colour, 15 g) lying flat; brown is pushed 24 mm into U, black into V, grey into W. Each lead lies on the table in a bow to the left: it leaves the gland heading straight forward (+x), swings out to 6.4 cm left of its gland position about 9 cm from the gland, and comes back to enter its socket straight. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Measured with a ruler and a photo; each plug carries tape marks 8 mm and 15 mm from its tip. A plug is in a socket when it is lined up with it (centre within 8 mm of the socket's centre line sideways, pointing into it within 25 degrees, its centre at most 5 mm above the opening's top) and its 8 mm mark is inside the face; it is home when its 15 mm mark is inside too. The plugs are measured once, when the robot, having touched a plug or lead (sim: a robot point within 2 mm), has been clear for 1 s: no part of either robot within 20 mm of the terminal box, the gland or any lead (plug or cable), and no plug moving more than 1 mm over that second. In the real trial the operator measures 1 s after the robot has moved clear (no part of it within 20 mm of the box, gland or leads): a photo of the plugs' depth marks taken at that moment, read afterwards, gives each plug's socket and depth, before the supply is switched on; that measurement is what is scored. If the robot comes back within 20 mm, the measurement is dropped and the supply goes off; the next one, after 1 s clear again, replaces it. Score 0 with no measurement, or unless each plug was in a different socket and the order reverses the motor: two leads exchanged relative to the start (an odd permutation; the start order and its two cyclic shifts score 0). Then 1.0 if all three were home and the belt has carried the tote wholly past the green (forward) line (100 mm forward); otherwise 0.5. The supply is switched on only if the measurement has all three plugs home; the motor then runs forward for an odd order and backward for an even one, moving the tote at 0.1 m/s. The trial ends early once the score has been 1.0 for 1 s.
reset_notes: Pull the three plugs out, push brown into U, black into V and grey into W until the 15 mm mark is hidden (24 mm in), lay each lead in its bow to the left as in the setup, bring the tote back to the centre of the belt between the lines, and turn the disc's stripe to the top. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Not simulated electrically: motor direction is computed from the lead order (odd permutation = forward). Leads: rigid 2 cm segments, fully plastic. Plugs: rigid boxes held only by socket walls and friction (no grip, contacts or latch). Simulated plugs creep up to about 0.3 mm/s for a few seconds after release (about 1.3 mm), so depth is scored once, 1 s after the robot has moved clear. Real ones should not: each socket's sprung side contact grips the pin (reasoned, untested on hardware).
